A content delivery network is a system of computers spread across many cities that store copies of websites and videos so people nearby can load them quickly. Normally, every request travels to one origin server, the single main computer where a website's original files live. If that server sits far away, pages load slowly, especially for large files like videos or images. To fix this, copies of the content get placed at edge locations, smaller storage points positioned closer to where people actually are, in different countries and regions. When someone requests a page, the network first checks whether a nearby edge location already has a saved copy. If it does, that's called a cache hit, meaning the answer comes back instantly without bothering the distant origin server at all. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries holding copies of popular books so no one has to travel to the one national archive every time they want to read something. Only when no nearby copy exists does the request travel further, fetch the content, and store a copy locally for next time. This setup reduces waiting time, eases pressure on the origin server, and keeps things working even during busy periods or partial outages. It quietly powers most fast-loading websites, streaming services, and apps used every day.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer holding a website's true files | Everything ultimately comes from here |
| Edge location | A nearby storage point holding copies of content | Brings information physically closer, cutting delay |
| Cache hit | A successful request answered by a stored copy | Means faster loading and less strain on distant systems |
| Content delivery network | The whole network connecting origin and edge locations | Makes modern fast, reliable browsing possible |
